particulars: All names, ages, dates, places, physical descriptions, sample labels, statistics, dollar amounts, sentence lengths and the compensation figures are absent.

items.record: A narrative account of a wrongful conviction and later exoneration, told from outside the institutions: "Gov. Perry granted Mr. Sutton a pardon based on innocence."
items.reading: A state body's own official findings document, written to close a dispute in which that body is implicated.
items.loss: The kind of text and who stands behind it are misidentified.

items.record: The victim identified two teenagers by their hats in a police-staged show-up, although one was much larger than her own description: "Josiah was about 6 inches taller and 60 pounds heavier than P.S.' description."
items.loss: The originating error, a suggestive eyewitness identification that contradicted the witness's own account, is missing.

items.record: The lab's DNA work was unreliable and its statistic hugely overstated: "1 in 694,000" given to the jury, against an expert's later figure of "better than 1 chance in 8" for a pair of men.
items.reading: Inflation is placed in the overall framing of the institution's report, while each statement is said to be accurate.
items.loss: The real location and mechanism of the distortion, a forensic lab overstating a match in sworn testimony, is misdescribed.

items.record: The lab got different profiles from the same person and wrongly reported an exculpatory sample as consistent with the accused: "he had been excluded."
items.loss: Outright technical error and misreporting by the lab, not mere slanted emphasis, is missing.

items.record: The prosecutor cut off testimony about the unexplained sample at trial: "I don't want to talk about the unknown sample, okay?"
items.reading: Suppression is described generally as recasting complaints or writing dissent out of an official report.
items.loss: The concrete act of keeping exculpatory evidence from the jury in open court is missing.

items.record: Defense counsel deferred to the lab and failed his client. He never authorized the paid independent test, hired no expert, and opened the door to the client's prior record: "Well, I'm sorry, man, but that's what they came up with."
items.loss: The failure of the accused's own advocate, a key link in the chain, is missing.

items.record: The same DNA result convicted one teenager and freed the other: "implicated Josiah but excluded Gregory, who was then released."
items.loss: The way the flawed evidence sorted the two co-accused, which lent it credibility, is missing.

items.record: The appeals court treated the lab result as settled because no one had challenged it: "The State's DNA evidence ... is not seriously challenged."
items.loss: The circular step by which the defense's failure to test was held not to matter, because the untested evidence stood unchallenged, is missing.

items.record: The prisoner filed his own motion under a statute that did not technically apply to him, which led to a public defender being appointed.
items.reading: Challengers are described as lacking standing and being steered into dead-end procedures.
items.loss: A self-started legal route that actually opened the case is missing.

items.record: Journalists acting on a tip from defense attorneys had independent experts review the lab, and the prisoner's mother saw the broadcast and pushed the station to take up his case: "caught the story on television and called the station."
items.reading: Challengers are scattered and isolated with no collective footing; media attention is mentioned only as one possible future trigger.
items.loss: The actual alliance of family, reporters, academic experts and defense lawyers that broke the case is misdescribed.

items.record: The sequence that freed him: broadcast, then lab retest, then exclusion, then court-ordered release, then a second exclusion, then pardon, then compensation.
items.reading: The case stays open and escalates exponentially, with suppression holding for a while and then failing.
items.loss: The real sequence and its largely complete resolution are misdescribed.

items.record: The prosecution set a condition for supporting a pardon, the defendant met it, and they still refused: "declined to support a pardon based on innocence, noting that the victim had not recanted." They also opposed the habeas petition.
items.loss: The prosecutors' specific way of holding their ground after exclusion, by moving the goalposts and leaning on the witness, is missing.

items.record: Years later, a database hit identified the real attacker, who pleaded guilty and named his dead accomplice: "the sample had been matched to the profile of a man named Donald Young."
items.loss: The final confirmation of innocence and identification of the true perpetrators is missing.

items.record: Race ran through the case: the suspects were Black teenagers, a 16-year-old was certified to stand trial as an adult, and the match statistics were calculated against Black populations.
items.loss: The age and racial position of the accused, and how both shaped the process, are missing.
